description: Test your knowledge of MI3.1-9 | Bloodstream & Cardiovascular Infections.

cards.text: What is molecular mimicry in rheumatic fever and how does it cause cardiac damage?
cards.answer: Antibodies against Group A Streptococcus M-protein cross-react with cardiac myosin, valve endothelium, and neuronal antigens due to shared antigenic epitopes. This triggers an autoimmune attack on the heart, causing pancarditis and valvulitis.

tip.tip: GABHS M-protein looks like host cardiac proteins to the immune system — mistaken identity leads to self-attack.

cards.text: Why does rheumatic fever develop only after pharyngeal GABHS infection and not skin infection?
cards.answer: Pharyngeal GABHS strains express specific M-protein serotypes (M1, M3, M5, M6, M14, M18, M19, M24) with epitopes cross-reactive to cardiac tissue. Skin strains lack these pathogenic M-protein types.

tip.tip: Throat strains = cardiac killers. Skin strains = safe. Location + strain type matter.

cards.text: Define Aschoff body and name the characteristic cell type found within it.
cards.answer: Aschoff body is a perivascular granuloma with central fibrinoid necrosis, surrounded by Anitschkow cells (modified macrophages with caterpillar/wavy chromatin) and multinucleate giant cells. It is pathognomonic for rheumatic fever.

tip.tip: Anitschkow cells = caterpillar chromatin. They're the smoking gun of RF histology.

cards.text: List the five major criteria of the revised Jones Criteria (2015) for diagnosing first-episode rheumatic fever.
cards.answer: CANES: Carditis (pancarditis; new murmur), Arthritis (migratory polyarthritis of large joints), Nodules (subcutaneous, painless), Erythema marginatum (serpentine rash), Sydenham's chorea (involuntary movements, female predominance).

tip.tip: CANES spells the five major criteria. Carditis is most important; chorea is late and neurological.

cards.text: What is the latent period between pharyngeal GABHS infection and the onset of rheumatic fever?
cards.answer: 2–4 weeks after the acute pharyngitis resolves before RF symptoms manifest. This latent period reflects the time needed for immune sensitization and cross-reactive antibody formation.

tip.tip: 2–4 weeks gap: strep throat appears healed, then RF strikes. Molecular mimicry takes time.

cards.text: How do you interpret an elevated ASO titre in the context of suspected rheumatic fever?
cards.answer: ASO > 200 Todd units (adults) or > 333 Todd units (children <5 years) is significant. Serial rising titres are more meaningful than a single reading. High ASO alone is not diagnostic; it must be combined with clinical criteria.

tip.tip: ASO = Antistreptolysin O. High titre = past strep exposure. Rising titre = recent infection.

cards.text: Distinguish between acute and subacute infective endocarditis in terms of onset, causative organisms, and valve involvement.
cards.answer: Acute IE: rapid onset (days–weeks), aggressive organisms (e.g., S. aureus), infects normal valves, high mortality. Subacute IE: insidious onset (weeks–months), less virulent organisms (e.g., viridans streptococci), usually infects abnormal or damaged valves.

tip.tip: Acute = fast + violent + healthy valve. Subacute = slow + sneaky + damaged valve.

cards.text: Name three major complications of acute rheumatic fever and explain why secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin is essential.
cards.answer: Complications: pancarditis (acute phase), rheumatic heart disease/RHD (chronic valvular scarring; mitral stenosis most common in India), increased IE susceptibility on scarred valves. Secondary prophylaxis prevents recurrent strep infections that worsen valvular damage with each episode.

tip.tip: Each strep throat re-lights the fire. Benzathine penicillin monthly = firewall against recurrence and RHD progression.
